title: Collective memory of 9/11 remains broad while personal lifestyle change and terrorism worry are lower and confidence in government protection is partisan
source_unit: Gallup national poll conducted August 3-24, 2026, with anniversary trend comparisons from 2000-2021

observations.period: 2000-2026; 9/11 memory, personal change, terrorism worry, and confidence in government protection

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed in the August 2026 Gallup poll

collective_lifestyle_change.value: 64% say Americans permanently changed how they live because of 9/11, matching the high recorded at the 20th anniversary; 58% said this at the 10th anniversary and 53% at the fifth

personal_lifestyle_change.value: 28% say they personally permanently changed how they live because of 9/11, compared with 22% at the fifth anniversary and 28% at the 10th and 20th anniversaries

terrorism_worry.value: 37% worry a great deal or fair amount about being a victim of terrorism, compared with 36% in 2021, 45% in 2006, 58% immediately after 9/11, and 24% in 2000

government_protection_confidence.value: 55% have a great deal or fair amount of confidence that the government will protect them from terrorism, tying the low recorded in December 2015; this was 59% in 2021, 75% 15 years ago, and 88% immediately after 9/11

current_party_split_in_protection_confid.value: Confidence that government will protect people from terrorism is 78% among Republicans, 59% among independents, and 29% among Democrats; in 2021 the corresponding figures were 41%, 53%, and 80%

personal_change_subgroup_contrast.value: Across the combined 2021 and 2026 surveys, personal permanent change is reported more often by Hispanic adults (51%) and Black adults (35%) than White adults (22%), and by weekly religious attenders (40%) than those who seldom or never attend (22%)

observations.method: Repeated cross-sectional Gallup anniversary polling, with the latest national poll conducted August 3-24, 2026; measures compare collective and personal reported change, terrorism worry, and confidence in government protection across years and demographic or partisan groups.
observations.uncertainty: The surveys are not a panel and do not observe the same people over time. Reported lifestyle change is not a behavioral diary or administrative measure, and the time-series differences may reflect question wording, current events, recall, cohort replacement, or changing partisan composition. The reported sample size is rounded to nearly 3,000 in the publication.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with published comparisons by party identification, race and ethnicity, religious attendance, age, and urbanicity; combined 2021/2026 estimates are used for some subgroup contrasts.
observations.counterinterpretation: A durable collective narrative can coexist with limited personal behavior change because people may understand 9/11 as historically consequential without changing daily routines. Lower terrorism worry does not establish lower objective risk, and the partisan confidence reversal may reflect broader polarization of government legitimacy rather than terrorism-specific performance judgments.

boundary: This record adds a long-horizon cultural-memory, security-perception, and partisan legitimacy layer. It does not infer actual lifestyle behavior, terrorism incidence, government protection capability, causal effects of 9/11 memory, or respondent-level trajectories.
